name: Sri Krishna Matha, Udupi
deity: Krishna, worshipped as the child Bala Krishna holding a churning rod and rope
period: Founded in the 13th century by the philosopher Madhvacharya
dynasty: Founded by Madhvacharya; sustained by the Ashta Mathas
summary: In coastal Karnataka, the child Krishna is worshipped through a small silver-plated window of nine holes — the Navagraha Kitiki — in a temple founded by the great philosopher Madhvacharya and run to this day by the eight monasteries he established.

sections.history: The Sri Krishna Matha at Udupi was founded in the thirteenth century by Madhvacharya, the philosopher-saint who gave the world Dvaita Vedanta, the school of thought that holds the individual soul and the supreme reality to be eternally distinct. Tradition tells that Madhva obtained the image of the child Krishna from a lump of sacred gopichandana clay that had served as ballast on a ship saved from a storm off the Malpe coast; recognising the Lord within, he installed it at Udupi. To care for the worship he established eight monasteries — the Ashta Mathas — whose pontiffs to this day take turns serving the deity. This rotation, the Paryaya, hands the worship of Krishna from one matha's swami to the next every two years in a great festival, an institution unbroken for centuries that makes Udupi as much a living seat of philosophy and learning as a temple. The town grew around the matha into one of the foremost centres of Vaishnava thought in southern India.
sections.architecture: Unlike the soaring Dravidian temple-cities of the Tamil country, the Krishna Matha is a compact complex in the coastal Karnataka idiom — tiled roofs, timbered halls, and a great stepped tank, the Madhva Sarovara, beside it. The heart of the shrine is the image of Bala Krishna, the child Krishna, standing with a churning rod and rope in his hands, richly ornamented and worshipped facing west. The temple's most famous feature is the way the Lord is seen: devotees take darshan through a small silver-plated window pierced with nine holes, the Navagraha Kitiki, also remembered as the Kanakana Kindi. The surrounding mathas, halls for feeding pilgrims, and the tank complete a setting built for daily worship and for the crowds that a great pilgrimage centre draws, rather than for monumental scale.
sections.legends: The most beloved story of Udupi is that of Kanakadasa, a devotee of humble birth who was kept from entering the shrine. Standing at the rear wall he sang to Krishna in pure longing, and the Lord — so the tradition holds — turned around to face him and opened a crack in the wall so that his devotee could have darshan. That opening became the Navagraha Kitiki, the nine-holed window through which every pilgrim now sees Krishna, so that the Lord still faces the direction from which the outcast sang. The story is cherished across Karnataka as a parable that devotion, not birth, is what reaches God. The founding legend of the image itself — recovered from a ship's ballast of sacred clay and recognised by Madhva as Krishna — frames Udupi as a place where the divine arrives unlooked-for and is known only by the eye of true insight.
sections.festivals: Krishna Janmashtami, the birth of Krishna, is celebrated with great splendour, its festivities including the vibrant Vitla Pindi. The defining event of Udupi, however, is the Paryaya, held every two years, when the right to worship Krishna passes ceremonially from the outgoing matha to the incoming one amid processions and scholarly gatherings. Makara Sankranti, the annual Saptotsava, and the daily cycle of ritual, music, and the feeding of thousands in the matha's dining halls mark the temple's calendar, sustaining Udupi's reputation as much for its hospitality and its kitchens as for its worship.
sections.experience: A visit to Udupi is a visit to a living monastery as much as a temple. The town is compact and walkable, the matha at its centre ringed by the eight monasteries, bookshops, and the tank. Take darshan of Krishna through the Navagraha Kitiki, walk the corridors, and — as generations of pilgrims have — eat in the matha's dining hall, for Udupi cuisine takes its very name from this place. The coast is close by: Malpe beach and the rock island of St Mary's are a short drive, and the temple towns of coastal Karnataka lie along the road, making Udupi a natural centre for a journey through the Tulu Nadu country.

visit.timings: Open daily from early morning to night with several darshan and worship sessions and a midday break; festival days and Paryaya years are especially crowded. Confirm current timings before travelling.
visit.dressCode: Modest, traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; men are often asked to remove upper garments before entering the inner shrine, following local custom. Remove footwear before entry and behave respectfully within the living matha.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted, particularly around the sanctum and the Navagraha Kitiki; follow posted rules and the instructions of temple staff.
visit.gettingThere: Udupi is on the coast of Karnataka, well connected by rail and by the coastal highway; the nearest major airport is at Mangaluru, about 60 km to the south. The matha is in the heart of the town, within walking distance of the bus stand and railway approaches.
